result.question: What litigation involving the App Store does Apple disclose, and what outcomes does it describe?
result.answer:
Apple discloses one principal App Store litigation matter — the **Epic Games** lawsuit — along with a general note about broader antitrust investigations related to App Store terms.

**Epic Games Lawsuit**

Epic Games, Inc. filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (the "California District Court") against Apple alleging violations of federal and state antitrust laws and California's unfair competition law based on Apple's operation of its App Store [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002].

The California District Court originally found that certain provisions of Apple's App Review Guidelines violate California's unfair competition law and issued an injunction (the "2021 Injunction") enjoining Apple from prohibiting developers from including in their apps buttons, external links, or other calls to action directing customers to purchasing mechanisms other than Apple's in-app purchase system [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002]. Earlier filings note that the District Court ruled in favor of Apple on 9 out of 10 counts in Epic's claim and that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed the District Court's ruling on April 24, 2023 [0000320193-23-000077:part-ii--item-1-p001].

On January 16, 2024, Apple implemented a plan to comply with the 2021 Injunction and filed a statement of compliance with the California District Court [0000320193-25-000073:part-ii--item-1-p002]. On September 30, 2024, Apple filed a motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction [0000320193-25-000073:part-ii--item-1-p002].

On April 30, 2025, the California District Court found Apple to be in violation of the 2021 Injunction and issued the "2025 Injunction," which enjoined Apple from imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app, from restricting or limiting how developers guide consumers to purchases outside an app, or otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002]. The California District Court also denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California for a determination whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate [0000320193-25-000073:part-ii--item-1-p002]. Apple appealed the April 2025 decision to the Ninth Circuit [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002].

On December 11, 2025, the Ninth Circuit issued an order upholding the 2025 Injunction in part and modifying certain aspects to allow Apple to require parity in size, form, and placement between its in-app purchase and any links for consumers to make purchases outside an app [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002]. The Ninth Circuit also held that Apple can charge a commission on link-out purchases, and remanded to the California District Court to further amend or modify the 2025 Injunction consistent with the Ninth Circuit's order [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002]. As of the most recent filing, the deadline for Apple to file a petition for rehearing was March 2, 2026 [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002].

**Broader App Store Investigations**

Apple also discloses that it is subject to antitrust investigations in various jurisdictions relating to App Store terms and conditions, and that adverse findings could result in significant fines and required changes to its App Store business [0000320193-23-000106:item-1a-p024].

**Outcomes and Current Status**

To summarize the outcomes: Apple prevailed on 9 of 10 counts at the District Court level [0000320193-23-000077:part-ii--item-1-p001]; the District Court nonetheless issued the 2021 Injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to include external purchase links [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002]; the District Court subsequently found Apple in violation of that injunction and issued the broader 2025 Injunction while also referring Apple for potential criminal contempt proceedings [0000320193-25-000073:part-ii--item-1-p002]; and the Ninth Circuit partially upheld and partially modified the 2025 Injunction, allowing Apple to charge a commission on link-out purchases and to require parity in display, and remanded for further proceedings [0000320193-26-000006:part-ii--item-1-p002]. The matter remains ongoing as of the most recent filing.
